name: Central banks vs energy inflation
backstory: The Iran war cut oil supply and pushed up [[headline inflation]], so central banks have been trying to decide whether the price jump fades on its own or leaks into wages and services. Euro area inflation reached 4%, the Bank of England hiked to 4%, and the Fed sits at 3.875%. Fed officials such as Williams, Waller and Cook have all framed the debate around rates possibly rising and oil staying high.
today: The Fed's preferred gauge, the [[PCE price index]], rose 3.8% from a year earlier in October, matching forecasts, and third quarter [[GDP]] was revised up to 4.3%. That leaves the Fed's 3.875% rate barely above inflation, so policy is hardly tight, which is why commentary now says Wall Street's 2027 earnings hopes need an easing that inflation makes unlikely. A CNBC commentary argues that Kevin Warsh should hike instead of betting on a productivity boom the way Greenspan did, and households are already scaling back holiday plans because toys, food and travel cost more. In Europe, the Bank of France governor still expects growth despite recession talk, pointing to defense, aerospace and electricity.

name: AI trade jitters
backstory: The biggest AI-linked tech firms hold up so much of the S&P 500 that doubts about AI hit the whole market. Nvidia's CEO left on Nov 12, a selloff followed, official papers warned that AI [[valuation]]s look stretched, and the index fell four straight weeks. Then Nvidia's board approved Huang's return and the Nasdaq jumped 6.51% on Monday.
today: Nvidia gave back a big chunk of Monday's rally, and according to Vanda Research the gains of retail investors who bought the dip last week are now nearly all gone. Oracle and CoreWeave sank early and then bounced as the selloff eased before the close, so the day was volatile but ended less ugly than it began. Vance said he was assured Huang was not under a DOJ investigation, while a CNBC column says Treasury Secretary Bessent's about-face on Huang shows how unsettled the administration's stance on Nvidia and China is.

name: US midterms and the dollar
backstory: The midterms produced what headlines call a Democratic rout, and markets asked how divided government might change tariffs, spending and the dollar. The dollar then had its biggest rally since 2024, with headlines crediting hawkish Fed bets and not the election. It hit a 20-month high, its strongest since March 2025.
today: The dollar index slipped 0.07% to 103.74 after early strength faded. The dollar turned lower after the US announced plans for new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU, and as Treasury yields fell. Commentary now suggests the dollar may be peaking, and the Swiss franc gained as a safe haven. On Tuesday, consumer confidence jumped to 103.3 after the Democratic wins, though inflation worries persist.

name: Iran war and oil
backstory: The conflict began in early 2026 and cut global oil output by 12 mb/d in March, but prices stayed below records because stored oil filled the gap. The IEA says the Hormuz shock lifted the world's oil and gas import bill 25% to $1.6 trillion. Pump prices recently fell to their lowest level since March.
today: WTI crude rose 2.21% to 83.86, its second straight gain, because tension in the Middle East offset expectations for a global supply surplus. Energy and base metals stocks helped the Canadian TSX rebound. Meanwhile, Americans are cutting back on holiday plans as food, travel and gifts get more expensive, partly because of the war's energy shock.

name: Yen defense
backstory: A weak yen pushed Japan to intervene [sell dollars to buy yen] in the currency market, including a record $50 billion in one day. The BOJ's 1.25% rate is 2.625 percentage points below the Fed's 3.875%, which encourages selling yen to hold dollars. Japan's economy unexpectedly shrank in Q3 as energy costs bit.
today: USD/JPY was 159.32, down 0.04%, so the yen was little changed. The BOJ chief played down soft consumption data and signaled a near-term rate hike. Japan's inflation accelerated, and the country posted a sixth straight monthly trade deficit. A Reuters-style analysis says BOJ ambiguity on the path of hikes could tempt yen bears. In Friday's Asian session, the Nikkei fell 2.9% on chip and metals stocks.
